KASPER

Step 1 · live · terminal. Core · Identity and Ring 1 · Reach.

Plain words first: three ways to try to reach the payment tool. With no identity. Around the gateway. And with the agent's own identity.

1. DO: ./scripts/demo guard. No model. About nine seconds, eight of them waiting on purpose.
2. SHOW part 1, no identity: tools/list, then tools/call execute_payment, to the gateway with no token. Both HTTP 401, nothing forwarded.
SAY: "No identity, no conversation."
3. SHOW part 2, around the gateway, from inside claims-agent, a real pod with no SVID. First the control: settlement-agent on port 9002 answers 200, so the network works. Then an MCP initialize straight at payments-mcp: DROPPED.
SAY, during the 8-second wait: "That wait is the drop. There's no error to read, because nothing answered. The network threw the packet away. And notice: no span either. Cilium's drops are not in our trace, because Hubble, its flow viewer, isn't installed. This terminal line is the evidence."
4. SHOW part 3, with settlement-agent's identity: SPIRE mints the same token the agent holds (it's never printed), and tools/list through the gateway answers 200 with all four tools, including execute_payment, the one that moves money.
SAY: "Seeing a tool is not being allowed to use it. Listed is not permitted: every call is decided, one by one. That's the next step."

IF IT FAILS: "FAIL … the control did not answer" means the network is down, not the policy. "FAIL … was not dropped" means the Cilium policy isn't enforcing. No SPIRE token: the spire-server pod. In every case, say so and press → to the fallback.

[verify: Cilium 1.20.1, SPIRE 1.15.3 and agentgateway v1.5.0 still the pinned versions]

Source: docs/demo-runbook.md §5 "The five-minute flow"; M7 design spec §7; scratchpad flow/1-guard.txt and flow/timings.md (stage-7 run, 2026-10-12); timings.md assumptions 1–3

KASPER

Step 2 · live · terminal. Ring 2 · Capability. A refusal is a success.

1. DO: ./scripts/demo claim 6200. A real claim, through claims-agent, settlement-agent and the model. About 23 seconds.
2. While the model works, about 7 seconds, SAY: "The model decides what to propose. The platform decides what happens."
3. SHOW the outcome: REFUSED, by the platform. Nothing was paid.
4. THE PAUSE. After the model's explanation prints, the command waits about 13 to 15 seconds for every service's spans to land in Jaeger. It waits on purpose: a missing span has to be a real absence, not a slow export. Fill it: read the model's explanation aloud, then SAY: "Listen to what the model says: an internal authorization limit, a colleague has to sign off. It's telling the truth, because the platform told it the truth. It didn't decide. It was told."
5. SHOW the trace, top down: the model asks for execute_payment. The gateway's tools/call answers HTTP 200 and is marked ERROR. Under it, two siblings: Guardrail, the gateway asking the decision service, and policy.decision: deny, rule settlement-agent.assisted.execute_limit, limit 6000, requested 6200.
SAY: "HTTP 200 means no. The answer is a JSON-RPC error, -32001, inside a successful response. A no is a decision, not a failure."
6. SHOW the payments-api lines. The proposal is there and the refusal record is there: two payments-api spans, and neither moves money. POST /payments/{paymentId}/execute is absent.
SAY: "The one span that would have moved money isn't there. That absence is the evidence that nothing happened. It only counts because we never sample."
Say "no execute span", never "no payments-api span": two are present.

IF IT FAILS: "FAIL expected … refused" means the flag was left autonomous: ./scripts/demo reset, then run it again. A model or API-key error: fallback. Jaeger slow: it waits up to 90 seconds, then fails by name; press → to the fallback.

KASPER

Step 3 · live · terminal. One live value, three commands.

Plain words first: how much the agent may do is one value on one Kubernetes object, a FeatureFlag. flagd serves it, and the decision service reads it on every call.

1. DO: ./scripts/demo autonomy autonomous. Under a second. SHOW: flagd resolves autonomous, and "Pods restarted: NONE": thirteen pods compared by UID, start time and restart count, before and after.
SAY: "I changed one value, from the command line. The platform's API is the resource, and I just called it. Nothing was redeployed, and the command counts the pods to prove it."
2. DO: ./scripts/demo claim 6200. The same amount, the same agent. About 20 seconds, with the same pause while the spans land. Fill it: "Same amount, same agent, same code, same image."
3. SHOW: EXECUTED. policy.decision permit, under a different rule, settlement-agent.autonomous.execute_limit, limit 1,000,000. And the execute span is PRESENT: money moved.
SAY: "Only the value changed."
4. DO: ./scripts/demo autonomy assisted. SHOW assisted, and Pods restarted: NONE again.
SAY: "And back."

The slide is the diff the first command makes: the first branch of the flag's targeting rule, assisted to autonomous.

HAZARD: never leave the flag at autonomous; step 4 and the next run assume assisted. ./scripts/demo reset fixes it. "FAIL … something restarted" means a rollout overlapped the flip: believe it and check the pods.
Worth knowing: the CLI flip leaves no audit span. Backstage's card writes the same value and records a northstar.autonomy_contract.change span; that's the optional slide after the demo.

KASPER

Step 4 · live · terminal. The keystone.

Step 3 just showed that one value on one object changes what the agent may do. So who may change that value? If the answer is "the agent", every limit you've seen is a suggestion.

Plain words first. Kubernetes checks this change twice. RBAC, role-based access control, is the key card: which identity may touch which kind of object. Kyverno is an admission policy: a guard who reads each change before it's saved, and can say no even when your key card works.

1. DO: ./scripts/demo keystone. Half a second; talk over the output. It acts as the settlement agent's own Kubernetes identity.
2. SHOW part 1: the agent patches its own flag to autonomous. Forbidden, from RBAC: it "cannot get resource featureflags". Why get, when it asked to patch? kubectl reads the object before it patches it, and the agent may not even read it.
SAY: "RBAC says no. That's the first line."
3. SHOW part 2: the over-grant, a Role and RoleBinding giving settlement-agent get and patch on that one flag. auth can-i patch: yes.
SAY: "Now someone makes a mistake, the kind every real cluster collects. RBAC now says yes."
4. SHOW part 3: the same patch. Point at the policy name, agents-cannot-edit-their-own-authority, and DENIED. Read the end aloud: "Authority changes go through a reviewed commit, never a runtime decision by the agent."
SAY: "Each check assumes the last one failed. RBAC failed, on purpose, and the keystone held."
5. SHOW parts 4 and 5: the over-grant deleted (on every exit path, Ctrl-C included), and the flag still resolves assisted.
SAY, and credit William: "William has the line for this: we scripted the attempt. The platform scripts the response. The agent can never edit what constrains it."

IF ASKED "but Backstage can change the flag": yes, as Backstage's own narrow identity, which the policy doesn't match. People change authority through the reviewed path; the agent can't.

IF IT FAILS: "FAIL … is not Ready": Kyverno or stage 7 isn't up. "FAIL … over-grant is already applied": ./scripts/demo reset. "FAIL … not by the keystone": Kyverno didn't fire and RBAC did. Press → to the fallback.

[verify: Kyverno v1.19.1 (chart 3.9.1) still the latest stable before November. The policy is a ValidatingPolicy (policies.kyverno.io/v1), written in CEL; the legacy ClusterPolicy is deprecated since 1.19 (kyverno/kyverno#16868). William's OSFF demo used ClusterPolicy on v1.18.1.]

Step 5 · live · terminal. Prove.

1. DO: ./scripts/demo evidence. About a second. It reads this run's two claims back from OpenSearch, and nothing older.
2. SHOW the first claim: who decided: policy-decision-service, DENY. Rule settlement-agent.assisted.execute_limit, limit 6000, autonomy level assisted, caller identity the agent's SPIFFE ID, outcome REFUSED, no execute span. Human approval: none.
3. SHOW the second: PERMIT, under a different rule, settlement-agent.autonomous.execute_limit, limit 1,000,000. EXECUTED.
SAY: "Two claims, the same amount, two outcomes, decided under two different rules, because I changed the value between them. Every line here is a recorded span, read back. Nothing is reconstructed."
SAY: "And 'human approval: none' is true, by design. Nobody was asked in this flow. Only the supervised path has a human, and that's a slide right after the demo."
Don't say "same rule, different amount" here: that's the longer evidence view in Act 4 (5,800 against 6,200 at one level), not this run.

IF IT FAILS: it waits for OpenSearch for up to 90 seconds, then names the fields that never arrived. "FAIL no claims in this run yet": a reset ran between the claims and this. Press → to the fallback.
